summary: Leviticus 15 regulates ritual uncleanness connected with male discharges, semen, menstruation, and prolonged female bleeding. It traces how a status can extend through bodies, beds, seats, vessels, and touch, usually ending after washing and waiting, while a continuing male discharge and bleeding beyond the ordinary period require a seven-day count and offerings. The stated aim is to keep Israel’s uncleanness from defiling the tabernacle among them.
whyItMatters: The chapter places several bodily flows inside a sanctuary-access system shared by men and women. These conditions can make someone ritually unclean without making the body, the intercourse described, menstruation, or illness a moral fault.

context.author: The text presents these instructions as Yahweh’s words through Moses and Aaron; authorship and final composition are debated
context.audience: The children of Israel, both men and women, with priests receiving offerings after prolonged discharges
context.date: The laws are framed around Israel’s wilderness tabernacle; the date of final composition is debated
context.setting: Israel’s camp, where bodily states and contact affect access to the tabernacle

outline.heading: A man’s continuing discharge and contact effects
outline.note: Beds, seats, bodies, saddles, and vessels touched in relation to the discharge receive stated washing or disposal rules.

outline.heading: Cleansing after the male discharge ends
outline.note: Seven days, washing in running water, and two bird offerings complete the process.

outline.heading: Semen and intercourse
outline.note: Washing and uncleanness until evening follow an emission, affected fabric, or intercourse.

outline.heading: Menstruation and transferred uncleanness
outline.note: The woman’s seven-day status affects those who touch her or the places where she lies and sits.

outline.heading: Prolonged bleeding and restoration
outline.note: An out-of-cycle or extended discharge remains unclean while it lasts, followed by seven days and two offerings.

outline.heading: Protecting the tabernacle and summarizing the law
outline.note: The conclusion gathers male and female cases under the need not to defile God’s dwelling among Israel.

keyVerses.text: “‘When he who has a discharge is cleansed of his discharge, then he shall count to himself seven days for his cleansing, and wash his clothes; and he shall bathe his flesh in running water, and shall be clean.
keyVerses.why: Cleansing after the continuing male discharge includes a seven-day count, clothes washing, and bathing in running water.

keyVerses.text: If a man lies with a woman and there is an emission of semen, they shall both bathe themselves in water, and be unclean until the evening.
keyVerses.why: Intercourse with an emission creates temporary ritual uncleanness and requires bathing, without naming a moral offense.

keyVerses.text: “‘Thus you shall separate the children of Israel from their uncleanness, so they will not die in their uncleanness when they defile my tabernacle that is among them.’”
keyVerses.why: The chapter states its purpose as preventing uncleanness from defiling the tabernacle.

questions.question: What kind of male “discharge” does the opening section describe?
questions.answer: The opening describes a bodily discharge and its ritual effects without naming a modern medical condition. It distinguishes the status associated with the discharge from the seven-day cleansing process begun after the discharge has ended.

questions.question: Does uncleanness spreading through touch mean the chapter teaches germ theory?
questions.answer: The text says that beds, seats, touch, spit, saddles, and carried objects can extend ritual uncleanness, with washing and an evening limit in many cases. It gives rules for sacred status but no account of microbes, infection, or a medical mechanism.

questions.question: Why is an earthen vessel broken while a wooden one is rinsed?
questions.answer: The law requires a touched earthen vessel to be broken and a wooden vessel to be rinsed. It gives no explanation for treating the materials differently, so the distinction is certain while its rationale remains unstated.

questions.question: Are semen and sexual intercourse treated as moral sins?
questions.answer: Verses 16-18 require washing and uncleanness until evening after an emission of semen, including intercourse between a man and woman, but name no wrongdoing and require no sacrifice in these cases. The consequence is temporary ritual status, not a moral condemnation of sex.

questions.question: What happens during the woman’s ordinary menstrual period?
questions.answer: She is in ritual impurity for seven days. What she lies or sits on becomes unclean, and people who touch her or those places receive a temporary status, generally with washing and bathing; the passage does not call menstruation sinful.

questions.question: How is bleeding outside or beyond the ordinary period handled?
questions.answer: The woman remains unclean for as long as the discharge lasts, and her bed and seat carry the same status. When it stops, she counts seven days, then brings two birds on the eighth day for priestly offerings and atonement.

questions.question: Why are sin offerings used for prolonged discharges if the person is not accused of sin?
questions.answer: For both the man and woman, the birds are offered after the discharge has ended, and the text says atonement is made for the discharge or its uncleanness. No immoral choice is alleged, showing that the WEB’s “sin offering” label has ritual cleansing work here beyond punishment for personal guilt.

questions.question: Why does verse 31 warn that people could die in their uncleanness?
questions.answer: The danger named is defiling Yahweh’s tabernacle, which stands among the people. Bodily uncleanness itself is not presented as a capital crime; the warning concerns bringing that status across the sanctuary boundary instead of following the separation and cleansing rules.

glossary.def: A flow from the body that creates ritual uncleanness under the cases in this chapter.
Water specified for bathing after a continuing male discharge ends.
Yahweh’s portable sanctuary among Israel, whose sacred boundary the purity rules protect.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: The preceding chapter describes the cleansing of people after a skin condition and the inspection and cleansing of affected houses. The closing distinction between clean and unclean now leads into rules for bodily discharges.

here.text: Discharges, semen, menstruation, and prolonged bleeding receive distinct rules for contact, washing, waiting, and offerings. The closing warning explains their connection to the tabernacle among Israel.

after.text: The next chapter turns to the annual cleansing of the sanctuary and community, recalling Aaron’s sons’ deaths and restricting entry within the veil.
